title: Mastery Challenge: Philosophy
objective: After this level you can demonstrate command of Philosophy Levels 1 to 99 across the whole tree.
summary: One question from each chapter, from the first traditions to knowledge, mind, morals, justice, freedom, God, hard choices and the good life. Every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: The Philosophy Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Ten questions, one from each chapter, from Nagasena’s chariot to Nozick’s machine. Level 1 asked what philosophy is; now show what it can do. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Philosophy: mastered
learned: How thinkers from Greece, China, India, Islam and Judaism opened the questions of what is real and who we are.
Why Hume, Kant, Gettier and Searle left knowledge and mind harder to pin down than they first look.
What rival views say about right, justice, freedom and God, with the strongest case on each side.
How to take a new big question through clarifying, a thought experiment and rival views.

questions.prompt: What does Nagasena’s chariot show about a person, on the Buddhist argument?

options.label: A lasting soul riding along inside a changing body
options.rationale: The argument denies any self over and above the parts.

options.label: The single most important part, which is the mind
options.rationale: No single part is the self.

options.label: Unreal in every sense, with nothing there at all
options.rationale: They’re conventionally real, like the chariot.

options.label: A name for parts working together, with no self beyond them

questions.explanation: Like a chariot, a person is conventionally real: a name for parts well arranged, nothing more.

questions.prompt: Hume argued that neither reason nor experience can justify “every event has a cause”. Where did Kant say that guarantee comes from?

options.label: The mind supplies cause as a form for all experience
Enough careful observation of causes in nature
options.rationale: That’s the route Hume had already closed.

options.label: Reason reaching past experience to things in themselves
options.rationale: Kant denied reason gives knowledge beyond experience.

options.label: God’s promise that our senses don’t deceive us
options.rationale: Kant looked to the mind’s own structure instead.

questions.explanation: Kant turned the question around: objects must conform to our knowledge, and the mind supplies concepts such as cause, so every event we meet has one.

questions.prompt: A friend argues: “Predicting from the past has always worked before, so it will keep working.” Why would Hume say this argument fails?

options.label: Predictions from the past have often failed
options.rationale: Hume’s point isn’t about track records.

options.label: Only proofs in mathematics count as reasoning
options.rationale: He allowed probable reasoning; this one just can’t do the job.

options.label: It assumes the future will resemble the past
Tomorrow’s sunrise can be proved by reason alone
options.rationale: Hume denied that: a sunless tomorrow implies no contradiction.

questions.explanation: An argument from experience already takes for granted that the future will resemble the past. Hume said custom, not reasoning, carries us forward.

questions.prompt: Critics of Searle’s Chinese room say the man is only one part, and the whole system understands Chinese. How did Searle answer?

options.label: He agreed the room as a whole understands
options.rationale: He rejected the systems reply.

options.label: The man could memorize the rules and still understand nothing
He said no machine of any kind could ever think
options.rationale: Brains are machines, he said, and brains think.

options.label: He added a fluent Chinese speaker to the room
options.rationale: That would change the case, not answer the reply.

questions.explanation: Searle let the man memorize the rulebook and do everything in his head: now he is the whole system, and he still doesn’t know what a single character means.

questions.prompt: Suppose an act is right only because God commands it. Which worry does the Euthyphro dilemma raise about that option?

options.label: Rightness would then exist independently of God
options.rationale: That’s the worry about the other horn.

options.label: Morality would look arbitrary: cruelty could be commanded
Moral truth would change from one culture to the next
options.rationale: That’s relativism, a different debate.

options.label: God could never know which acts are right
options.rationale: The dilemma doesn’t question God’s knowledge.

questions.explanation: On this horn, had God commanded cruelty for fun, cruelty would be right. Theists such as Robert Adams reply by rooting morality in a loving God’s nature; critics reply that the puzzle has only moved.

questions.prompt: Rawls’s difference principle allows inequality only if it helps the least advantaged. What did Nozick’s Wilt Chamberlain case say about any pattern like it?

options.label: It is too cautious; pick the highest average instead
options.rationale: That was Harsanyi’s objection.

options.label: Great wealth is power, so a pattern can protect liberty
options.rationale: That was Cohen’s reply to Nozick.

options.label: It is just only when everyone chose it freely
options.rationale: Nozick judged holdings by how they came about, not by a pattern.

options.label: Free exchanges keep upsetting it, so keeping it restricts liberty

questions.explanation: Nozick’s moral was that liberty upsets patterns: holding any pattern in place means forbidding free exchanges or undoing their results. Cohen replied that patterns can preserve liberty.

questions.prompt: Frankfurt’s Jones could not have done otherwise, yet Frankfurt judged him fully responsible. Why does that matter to the debate over determinism?

options.label: It proves that determinism is false
options.rationale: The case says nothing about whether determinism is true.

options.label: It shows Black, not Jones, is really to blame
options.rationale: Black never acted; Jones decided on his own.

options.label: Lacking alternatives alone wouldn’t rule out responsibility
It shows responsibility rests on flickers of freedom
options.rationale: That’s what Frankfurt’s critics argue.

questions.explanation: If Frankfurt is right, responsibility doesn’t require the power to do otherwise, so even if determinism removed our alternatives, that alone wouldn’t show we can’t be responsible.

questions.prompt: Read as an argument, how does the prisoner’s climb out of Plato’s cave fit the theory of Forms from Level 4?

options.label: The soul turns from the changing, seen world to Forms known by thought
The senses prove to be the surest guide to what is real
options.rationale: For Plato, the seen world is the den.

options.label: Form turns out to live only inside each thing
options.rationale: That was Aristotle’s rival view.

options.label: Knowledge is poured into a soul that had none
options.rationale: Socrates denied education works like that.

questions.explanation: The den is the world of sight; the climb is the soul rising to the world known by thought, where the Form of the Good is seen last. Aristotle and later empiricists rejected the two worlds.

questions.prompt: Counting lives alone gives the switch and the footbridge the same answer, yet many judge them differently. How does the doctrine of double effect explain the gap?

options.label: It counts the people on each track more carefully
options.rationale: The numbers are the same in both cases.

options.label: It asks whether the person harmed agreed to it
options.rationale: Consent isn’t what the doctrine turns on.

options.label: It forbids every act that leads to any death
options.rationale: It allows some foreseen harms.

options.label: It separates harm used as a means from a foreseen side effect

questions.explanation: At the switch, the death is a foreseen side effect; on the bridge, the stranger’s body is the means. Critics answer with the problem of closeness.

questions.prompt: Nozick’s experience machine suggests that something matters besides experience. That challenges the premise of Epicurus’s argument about death that _____.

options.label: good and bad require sensation
the gods do not care about us
options.rationale: That isn’t a premise of this argument.

options.label: death comes to everyone
options.rationale: Nozick doesn’t challenge that.

options.label: fear of death is common
options.rationale: That’s not a premise either.

questions.explanation: If something matters besides experience, then good and bad don’t lie wholly in sensation, and Epicurus’s first premise is in doubt.
